newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi minister urges industries to shape up.
newsitem.headline: Saudi minister urges industries to shape up.

text.p: A Saudi minister urged local industries on Tuesday to care more about international quality standards as the kingdom seeks to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), the official Saudi news agency (SPA) said.

Industry and Electricity Minister Hashem bin Abdullah bin Hashem Yamani told a local seminar on "industrial investment opportunities" he expected Saudi to join the world body in two years "after all measures and negotiations were over."
"The industrial sector has to care about international quality rules and about research and development activities," SPA quoted Yamani as the opening session.

"It has to introduce planning and quality control programmes to lower costs, has to care about (personnel) training and about increasing production capacity and has to make better use of time," he added.
"You also have to care about marketing and adopting marketing strategies based on" research of local and international market trends, he told the industrialists.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, is pushing hard for quick entry to the WTO and has pledged to make every effort to satisfy trading partners and observe the body's rules.
It is seeking membership as a developing country, which would give it a special transitional period to bring its legislation and practices into line with WTO rules.

The seminar, organised by Yamani's ministry, the chamber of industries in the eastern province, home to some of Saudi's leading petrochemical industries, and local research agencies, will discuss 16 investment projects worth two billion riyals ($5.3 billion) it added.
Many firms of Saudi's industrial and petrochemical giant Saudi Basic Industries Corp (SABIC) are concentrated in the eastern Red Sea coastal province.

Abdul-Rahman al-Jaafari, head of the Gulf Industrial Organisation consultancy, told the seminar the oil-rich Arab Gulf States had to invest $1.5 billion a year until the year 2025 on manufacturing industries to keep pace with current labour growth.

He said finding enough positions to meet growing job-seekers and redressing the current imbalance in employment structures were major challenges facing the Gulf Cooperation Council -- grouping Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates.
He said GCC nationals only formed three percent of the total workforce in these countries which rely on armies of Western expatriates and labourers to help them run their economies.

He said total value added by the local industries to their economies reached $19 billion dollars in 1994 from $3.6 billion in 1976. Their industrial exports increased to seven percent between 1991 and 1994 from 2 percent during 1976 and 1980.
